Column 3: A centuries old vampire gets really into video games because playing a character who can walk around in the sun is the closest thing they have to experiencing the day again in centuries.
Column 4:
The sunlight on the screen was the color of honey. 

Lysander’s fingers twitched against the controller, guiding his in-game avatar—a broad-shouldered farmhand with a laugh that gusted like summer wind—through a wheat field. Pixelated gold rippled under a digital sky so blue it ached. He’d forgotten that blue. Forgotten the way heat could pool in the hollow of a collarbone, or how dust motes danced in slanting daylight. Three hundred years since he’d seen it firsthand. Three centuries of shadows, of cramped rooms reeking of mothballs and blackout curtains. 

But here, in *Stardawn Valley*, he could pretend. 

The farmhand knelt to plant tulip bulbs. Lysander’s throat tightened. He remembered doing that once, in another life. His human hands caked with soil, sweat trickling down his neck as his sister teased him for fussing over “fragile little things.” The memory was frayed, eroded by time, but the game’s idle soundtrack—soft guitar strings, a humming chorus—stitched the fragments together. 

A notification blinked: *SunnyGurl92 wants to join your session!* 

He hesitated. Multiplayer was risky. But loneliness, he’d found, was sharper than sunlight. He hit *Accept*. 

“Dude, your farm is *epic*,” came a voice through the headset, bright and crackling with static. “How’d you get the sunflowers so big?” 

Lysander smiled. “Blood sacrifice.” 

SunnyGurl92’s avatar—a pink-haired chef in overalls—snort-laughed. “Hardcore. I just use fertilizer.” They spent the next hour trading seeds and bad jokes. She didn’t ask why he only played at night. He didn’t ask about the tremor in her hands when she mentioned her “offline” job at a hospice. The game’s perpetual noon stretched on, forgiving. 

At 4:57 a.m., Lysander’s skin began to prickle. Dawn lurked beyond the apartment’s sealed windows. “I have to go,” he said abruptly. 

“Wait! Let’s visit the mountain summit first. The sunrise there is insane.” 

His cursor hovered over *Exit Game*. Human cruelty was so mundane, so *accidental*. “...One minute.” 

They sprinted up the pixelated trail. The farmhand’s boots crunched pretend snow. At the peak, the screen softened into watercolor hues—pink, peach, amber. Lysander’s chest burned. He couldn’t tell if it was the vampire curse or grief. 

“Pretty, right?” SunnyGurl92 whispered. 

The first time he’d burned, age 24, he’d been chasing a stray lamb at dawn. There’d been no pain at first—just a brilliant white light, then centuries of darkness. Now, he stared at the simulated sunrise until his eyes stung. The farmhand lifted his pixel face to the sky, and Lysander let himself sway, just a little, imagining the warmth. 

He logged off as the in-game sun cleared the horizon. Outside, real daylight seeped through the curtains’ edges. Lysander retreated to his closet, laptop clutched to his chest. The farmhand’s laughter echoed in the dark, a secondhand ghost. 

He dreamed of tulips.

Column 3: A psychic alien who feeds on dreams comes to Earth for the first time. Turns out humans are the only sentients in the galaxy that have nightmares.
Column 4:
Zyrath’s tendrils trembled as they brushed the atmosphere, tasting the psychic residue of a billion sleeping minds. They had feasted across seven galaxies, sipping the pastel tranquility of dreams where sentients floated in serene, weightless joy. But Earth… Earth *reeked*. Its psychic aura coiled like smoke, acrid and jagged, laced with something Zyrath’s translator-cells struggled to name. Not fear. Not sorrow. Something that *burned*.  

The first nightmare hit as they phased through a suburban roof.  

A child’s scream. Teeth like shattered mirrors. A shadow with too many joints crawling up a wall. Zyrath recoiled, membranes stinging—until the aftertaste registered. Beneath the terror thrummed a metallic tang, rich and dark, vibrating with a depth no nectar-sweet dream had ever offered. They followed the thread downward.  

The woman thrashing in bed smelled of salt and unwashed hair. Clara, her mind hissed. Thirty-two revolutions around this yellow star. Five since the accident. The nightmare unfolded like rotting parchment: a minivan’s screech, a tiny shoe in rain-soaked asphalt, the ceaseless beep of a hospital monitor. Zyrath hesitated. To feed here felt profane, like drinking from an open wound.  

They drank anyway.  

It was a supernova in reverse—all that collapsing fury, that crushing weight of *what if* and *if only*. Zyrath’s bioluminescence flickered erratically as human neurochemicals flooded their system: cortisol sharp as broken glass, adrenaline like white-hot wires. They tried to pull away, but Clara’s psyche clung, desperate. Her grief wasn’t a static painting but a living thing, thrashing, *evolving*.  

By dawn, Zyrath huddled in her attic, quivering. They’d consumed rage that left phantom bruises, guilt that gnawed like stomach acid, shame sticky as blood. Yet when Clara woke, she breaked coffee, humming a fractured lullaby. She lived.  

The alien observed her for weeks. Humans, they realized, were creatures of paradox. They buried nightmares under daylight rituals—laughed with broken voices, kissed with trembling lips. Each night, Zyrath gorged, drunk on horrors that somehow *strengthened* these fragile beings. A soldier’s flashbacks carried the crispness of survival; a widow’s recurrent darkness pulsed with undimmed love.  

One midnight, Clara’s nightmare shifted. The hospital beep dissolved into a meadow. Her daughter’s laughter echoed from behind a birch tree, always just out of sight. “I know you’re not real,” Clara whispered in the dream, tears hot. “But stay.”  

Zyrath fed, and this time, the aftertaste was different. Bitter, yes, but beneath it, something like the first rain after wildfire.  

They never left Earth. The galaxy’s other species pitied humanity, these shrieking, bleeding dreamers. But Zyrath swam in their stormy seas, learning a truth no tranquil mind could grasp: nightmares were not poison. They were the price, the alchemy, the forge.  

When the next star-farer asked why Zyrath’s light now flickered charcoal and crimson, they answered:  

“You savor still waters. I found an ocean that burns.”

Column 3: Aliens take over the Earth. They then announce that they will be forcing the humans to work a ‘tyrannical’ 4 hours a day 4 days a week in exchange for basic rights like housing. Needless to say they are very confused when the humans celebrate their new alien overlords
Column 4:
The saucers descended on a Tuesday, obsidian and silent, blotting out the sun. When the Vorath emerged—tall, iridescent-skinned, their four eyes blinking in unison—they broadcast their demands in a voice like grinding stone. *“Your labor sustains us now. Four hours daily, four days weekly. Compliance grants shelter, sustenance, survival. Resistance is extinction.”*  
  
The crowd in Times Square gaped. Then someone laughed.  
  
It began as a stifled snort, then erupted into full-bodied howls. A woman hugged a stranger, tears streaking her face. “Four hours?” a man shouted, waving his phone. “I used to bill *twelve* for consulting!” The Vorath’s cranial ridges flushed crimson, a sign of agitation. Their High Overseer, Kl’ra, tilted her head, mandibles twitching. “Why do they… *rejoice*?” she asked her second, V’tik. “Our simulations predicted revolt.”  
  
The humans were already composing ballads. Memes of Vorath in party hats flooded TikTok. Unions demanded the aliens *formalize* the arrangement: “Make the four-hour day legally binding!”  
  
Kl’ra ordered a human brought aboard her ship—a midlevel marketing manager named Luis, still clutching a “THANK U, OVERLORDS!” latte. “Explain this… *gratitude*,” she demanded. Luis shrugged. “Before you came, I worked sixty-hour weeks. Couldn’t afford my apartment. My kid’s daycare cost half my salary.” He sipped his latte. “Now I garden. Teach her chess. You guys gave us *time*.”  
  
The Vorath exchanged glances. On their homeworld, productivity was sacred; citizens cycled through twenty-hour shifts, sustained by nutrient pastes, their worth measured in output. Leisure was decadence. Survival was earned through relentless toil.  
  
“You see this as *generosity*?” V’tik muttered.  
  
“We see it as not being exploited,” Luis said.  
  
Kl’ra’s exoskeleton paled. She’d intended to break them, to harvest their grit. Instead, she’d unearthed a fragility her algorithms hadn’t comprehended: a species so accustomed to being drained that a trickle felt like a flood.  
  
Later, watching humans picnicking in parks they’d once only hurried through, Kl’ra felt a pang of something alien. “Perhaps,” she mused to V’tik, “we underestimated their definition of tyranny.”  
  
“Or overestimated their tolerance for suffering,” V’tik replied.  
  
The Vorath recalibrated. They mandated “recreational intervals” and capped productivity metrics, baffled when humans used the extra hours to bake bread, write poetry, rebuild eroded communities. Resistance cells did form—not against the Vorath, but against attempts to revert to the old ways. “Keep your forty-hour hellscape!” graffiti read. “We’re thriving.”  
  
Kl’ra never admitted it, but she began lingering near Earth’s oceans at dusk, studying the way humans sat quietly, watching waves. Once, she downloaded a novel. *Ulysses*. She understood none of it, yet…  
  
“They’re *happy*,” she told V’tik.  
  
“A flaw?”  
  
“A revelation.”  
  
The Vorath’s conquest became a quiet revolution. Uprisings flickered on distant worlds when news spread: the humans, with their four-hour days, had somehow conquered *back*. Not through weapons, but by unshackling something in the Vorath’s own soul. Kl’ra’s reports grew poetic, then personal. She resigned her post, requested asylum.  
  
“I wish to learn,” she told Luis, “how to sit. How to… *be*.” He taught her to sip coffee slowly, to name the stars without mapping them. The galaxy’s most efficient overlords became its most reluctant philosophers, whispering a dangerous truth: maybe survival wasn’t everything. Maybe there was more.  
  
The saucers still hover, but now, they cast shadows that feel like shelter.

Column 3: Humanity is visited by a cosmic horror the likes of which has only been seen in Lovecraftian horror. In desperation, Earth throws everything we have at it, and, miraculously, the human race has killed a God. Somewhere in a realm beyond our understanding, the other gods speak of the event.
Column 4:
The sky wept ash the day we killed a god.  

They called it Xal’thar, a name scraped from static between radio telescopes. It arrived as a bruise on the horizon, a tumor of tentacles and eyes that drank starlight. Its voice was a bassline in our bones, promising dissolution. Armies shattered. Cities folded like origami into its maw. We were ants scuttling beneath a boot—until President Ruiz, her voice frayed on live TV, said, “Throw it all. *Everything*.”  

Nuclear arsenals. Hypersonic rails. AI-piloted drones sharp as razors. They dissolved like sugar in water. Dr. Elena Li, who’d once studied dementia, noticed the pattern: Xal’thar consumed *order*. Machinery. Algorithms. “It’s eating our *certainty*,” she whispered. Her hands shook as she proposed the alternative—a neural net, wired into every surviving human. A weapon of chaos. Of *dreams*.  

We huddled in bunkers, in subway tunnels, in forests singing with wildfires. Electrodes clung to our temples. “Think of grief,” Li urged. “Of love. Of the *mess*.” The system harvested it all—the man in Oslo cradling his dead dog, the girl in Mumbai humming a lullaby to her brother, the thousand million private hungers. We became a storm.  

Xal’thar recoiled. For the first time, its tentacles *twisted*, eyes dimming. It screamed in a frequency that burst dams, that crumbled limestone. But we screamed louder.  

When it died, the silence was a held breath.  

---  

Somewhere else, in a vault between entropy and time, the gods convened.  

“A *mortal* wound,” hissed Yg’nath, whose form was a calculus of spirals. Its voice dissolved into echoes: *mortal, mortal, mortal*.  

The assembly shuddered. Their shapes defied geometry—a nest of black veins, a sigh with teeth, a hunger that wore supernovas as jewelry.  

“They weaponized… *ambiguity*,” said The One Who Gnaws, tendrils flickering with disdain. “How?”  

Memories were exchanged, viscous and reluctant. A species that built cathedrals of questions. That named constellations after dead lovers. That clung to fragile meanings in a meaningless void.  

The Starving Maw, eldest of them, pulsed slowly. “We assumed their chaos made them weak. But it *bent*. It *folded*.” A pause, thick with unease. “Xal’thar’s essence is… *scattered*. They have tasted godhood.”  

A colder silence now.  

“Do they know?” whispered The Dread That Sings in Marrow.  

The Maw’s light dimmed. “They will.”  

---  

On Earth, survivors emerged, squinting at a sun that seemed too gentle. Li knelt in the ruins of Geneva, a neural node still glued to her wrist. Her toddler’s laughter looped in her head—a file she’d uploaded to the net. *Was that you, mi vida?*  

In the soil beneath her, something glistened. Not shrapnel. Not bone. A shard of *night*, vibrating softly. When she touched it, visions erupted: vast intelligences recoiling, a chorus of dread. *What are we now?*  

Above, satellites blinked. The nodes were still active. Still listening.  

Li smiled, dizzy.  

Somewhere, a god shuddered.

Column 3: Instead of the Monkey’s Paw, you find the Clown’s Nose, which instead of granting your wish in the worst way possible will grant it in the funniest way.
Column 4:
**The Clown’s Nose**  

Eleanor found it tucked between a taxidermied ferret and a ceramic unicorn in the back of Granny Mae’s Thrift Shoppe—a rubber clown nose, crimson and glossy, with a tag that read *“Laughter Guaranteed! (Or Your Soul Back!”)*. The cashier, a woman with mothball-scented hair, hissed, “Careful, dear. Last owner joined a cult. *Sober* one.” Eleanor, two months behind on rent and freshly dumped via Post-It, bought it for 50 cents.  

That night, she squeezed the nose. It honked.  

“I wish I had rent money,” she muttered.  

The ceiling exploded.  

Not with cash, but with rubber chickens. Dozens rained down, each squawking, *“CLUCK-A-DOODLE-DOO!”* Eleanor pried one open—a $20 bill fluttered out. Another—a roll of quarters. Another—a coupon for 10% off existential despair. By dawn, she’d harvested $1,200.37 and a newfound fear of poultry.  

“Funny,” she told the nose. “But *why chickens*?”  

It honked again.  

——  

Wish two: “I want someone to love me.”  

The doorbell rang. A mime stood there, striped shirt, tear painted on his cheek. He handed her a balloon poodle. When she laughed, he mimed a heart exploding. They shared wine—he pantomimed chugging, she actual-chugged. By midnight, they slow-danced to silent music, his hands shaping an invisible radio playing *Careless Whisper*. Eleanor’s ex had never serenaded her via imaginary saxophone.  

But when she woke, the mime was gone. In his place: a life-sized origami swan with “*MERCI*” inked on its wing. The nose, smug on her nightstand, honked.  

——  

“Undo it!” she yelled, clutching the nose. “I want my normal, *boring* life back!”  

Her apartment quaked. The walls peeled into striped tent fabric. Her couch sprouted popcorn. Her tabby, Mr. Whiskers, materialized in a tiny clown car, honking the horn with his paw. A call from her principal: “Eleanor, why is the schoolhouse *literally* a big top?”  

She stormed outside. Neighbors juggled hedgehogs. Fire hydrants sprayed confetti. A cop pulled her over for “excessive whimsy.”  

“Fix this!” she screamed at the nose.  

It honked.  

——  

Eleanor sat on a sidewalk, watching a pug skateboard in a tutu. The sun dipped, painting the chaos gold. She’d spent months aching for control—over bills, love, her crooked bangs. Now, the world was a punchline, and she… *wasn’t laughing*.  

She squeezed the nose. “Okay, fine. What’s the joke?”  

Silence. Then, a whisper: *“You.”*  

Eleanor blinked. Then snorted. Then cackled, wild and loud, until her ribs ached. The nose warmed in her hand, melting into goo. Around her, the circus faded. Tents became brick; confetti, leaves. Mr. Whiskers reappeared, licking his paw, unimpressed.  

On her desk, the nose—now ordinary rubber—sat beside a note: *“Laughter’s just fear, upside-down. – Marcel (The Mime)”*  

Eleanor pinned the nose to her coat. That Friday, she took her students to the park, taught geometry via hula-hoops. When rain drenched them, she honked the nose, and the puddles sprouted rainbows.  

The principal called it “unorthodox.”  

The kids called it magic.

Column 4:
In the bowels of an ancient castle, shrouded in the thick mist of a forgotten forest, there resided Vladimir, a vampire whose age was marked not by wrinkles but by the slow petrification of his heart. For centuries, the sun had been a mere memory, its warmth a forbidden caress against his marble skin. 

Vladimir had seen empires rise and fall, watched from the shadows as the world danced through centuries of light and darkness, always a spectator, never a participant. His existence was a monochrome tableau, painted in shades of night. That was until the night Aleksandra arrived, carrying a curious box under her arm—a gaming console, she called it, a treasure trove of the sunlit world.

"You need to see this, Vlad," she insisted, her eyes gleaming with excitement. The modern world baffled Vladimir, with its rapid pulsing life, so unlike the slow, deliberate cadence of his own eternal waltz. But Aleksandra, with her infectious enthusiasm, had a way of making the new seem less formidable.

She set up the console with practiced ease, flipping switches and pressing buttons until the large screen flickered to life. "Watch," she said, handing him a controller, an odd contraption of buttons and joysticks.

The game she chose was called "Sunlit Odyssey," an adventure set in a world so saturated with light and color that Vladimir felt a pang in his chest—a phantom pain from a heart that hadn't beaten in centuries. The character he controlled was a young hero, vibrant and alive, dashing through sun-drenched fields and over sparkling rivers under a sky so blue it ached.

With each press of the button, Vladimir guided the hero through quests and battles, each victory a small defiance against his nocturnal bondage. The game offered him a palette of sensations he hadn't felt in ages—the warmth of the sun, the brush of the wind, the thrill of daylight. 

As the hours slipped by, unnoticed and irrelevant, Aleksandra watched Vladimir transform. His usual stoic demeanor gave way to expressions of wonder, frustration, and triumph. For the first time in countless nights, his world was awash with color, emotions stirring within him that he thought were long dead.

"It feels like I'm alive again," Vladimir confessed quietly during a pause, his eyes not leaving the bright world trapped behind the screen. Aleksandra smiled, a soft, knowing curve of her lips.

"I thought it might help," she replied. "To walk in the sun, even if just in this little way."

Night after night, Vladimir returned to the console with religious fervor, exploring every game Aleksandra brought him. Each game was a different life, a different adventure, each sunrise on the screen a bittersweet reminder of what he had lost and what he had found.

In the pixelated glow of his new day, Vladimir discovered a bridge between his eternal night and the ever-spinning world of the living. The games did not cure his longing, but they dulled the edge of his solitude, clothing him in the borrowed light of a thousand virtual suns, teaching an old vampire new ways to dream.

Column 3: A psychic alien who feeds on dreams comes to Earth for the first time. Turns out humans are the only sentients in the galaxy that have nightmares.
Column 4:
In the silvery gleam of Earth’s moon, Vaznek hovered just beyond the atmosphere, his form shrouded in celestial mist. As a dream-feeder from Zantris IV, his survival hinged on the ethereal sustenance of dreams. Across the galaxy, dreams were universally soft and sweet, rich with hope and the mundane contentment of life. But Earth, a blue speck teeming with complex life, pulsed with a strange, alluring energy.

For centuries, Vaznek had skimmed the surface of the cosmos, feeding from a thousand different minds. Yet none offered the sharp, intoxicating spice he now sensed in the dreams beneath him. With a ripple of anticipation, Vaznek descended, invisible, intangible, and insatiably curious.

His first encounter was a child, no more than six Earth years old. The boy’s dreamscape was vibrant, a playground of endless joy. But as Vaznek drew closer, the scene twisted suddenly into darkness. Toys turned to monstrous figures, laughter morphed into cries, and the ground itself seemed to swallow the child whole.

Vaznek recoiled. The taste was bitter, laced with raw fear, yet beneath that, a richness unlike any he had tasted. It was the flavor of nightmares, an anomaly unique to this world.

Eager to understand, Vaznek ventured deeper into the labyrinth of human consciousness. He flitted from one mind to another, each dream a world unto itself, each nightmare a revelation. He witnessed wars and losses, monsters and abysses, fears both existential and trivial. Unlike anything in the known galaxy, these humans wove tapestries of terror and beauty, their nightmares as vivid as life itself.

One particular dream caught his essence—a young woman walking alone on a deserted street. The shadows around her pulsed with unseen threats, her heart raced, each step echoing in the empty night. Yet as the fear crescendoed, Vaznek felt a surge of something else—strength, resilience. The woman turned to face her shadows, and the streetlight revealed her determined eyes.

Vaznek realized that these nightmares were not just fears; they were trials, crucibles in which humans forged their spirits. Each nightmare was a story of overcoming, of facing the dark and emerging stronger.

Days turned to weeks, and Vaznek, once a mere observer, found himself changed by the dreams he devoured. No longer content to float on the fringes of minds, he sought the darkest of nightmares, understanding them, absorbing their lessons.

When Vaznek finally left Earth, he carried with him more than the memories of flavors. He bore a new understanding of fear and strength, of the fragile yet resilient nature of sentient beings. Earth had offered him not just sustenance, but a gift—the knowledge that in the terrifying tapestry of nightmares, there lay hidden threads of incredible courage and hope.

As his form faded from the Earth’s realm, merging with the stars, Vaznek looked back at the glowing planet. He had fed on its dreams, but in return, it had enriched him with a new depth, a complexity to his existence that he would carry across the cosmos, forever altered by a planet where nightmares were as vital as the dreams themselves.

Column 3: Aliens take over the Earth. They then announce that they will be forcing the humans to work a ‘tyrannical’ 4 hours a day 4 days a week in exchange for basic rights like housing. Needless to say they are very confused when the humans celebrate their new alien overlords
Column 4:
When the skies finally opened up, revealing fleets of gargantuan ships, a shiver ran through the spine of humanity. People clutched their loved ones close, peering skyward as the towering silhouettes blotted out the sun. The world braced for annihilation, for enslavement, for a fate worse than extinction. 

Instead, an unexpected decree echoed through the streets and valleys of Earth: "In exchange for basic rights such as housing and sustenance, all capable humans will submit to four hours of labor per day, four days per week." This commandment was issued by Zorlax, the Supreme Commander of the Galactic Federation, his voice a metallic hum vibrating through every television and radio on the planet.

Chaos did not ensue. Rather, a puzzled murmur spread across the globe. Offices, factories, and homes filled with hushed, incredulous voices. Could this truly be the harsh decree of their new alien overlords? Was this the feared subjugation?

In New York City, Maria Gonzalez turned off her aging television, which flickered with the image of the great Zorlax. She looked over at her two roommates, cramped in their tiny apartment, and a grin spread across her face. “Four hours a day?” she laughed, shaking her head in disbelief. “That’s it?”

Her roommate, Jay, who had been juggling two jobs just to make rent, let out a whoop of joy. “I’m going to have time to actually see the sun on weekdays!”

In a small town in India, Rajiv closed his little grocery shop early, excitement bubbling within him. He rushed home, the words of the aliens spinning in his mind. Only four hours, four days a week? After years of toiling from dawn to dusk, the prospect felt like a breath of fresh air. That evening, his family sat together, discussing what they would do with all their newfound free time. His daughter wanted to start painting again; his son talked about finally starting his own tech project.

In Paris, Eloise, a single mother, wiped a tear from her eye as she hugged her young son. The relentless grind of her three part-time jobs had left her perpetually exhausted, her dreams of writing novels gathering dust on a shelf. Now, she could write, she could dream, she could live.

As weeks turned into months, the human spirit adapted. Parks filled with people reading, playing, and resting under the afternoon sun. Cafés buzzed with aspiring entrepreneurs and artists sharing ideas and laughter. The dreaded occupation had unwittingly birthed a renaissance of culture, passion, and leisure.

Zorlax observed this with growing confusion. His tentacled brow furrowed as he watched humans embracing their families in the middle of what should have been a workday. “They should be cowering,” he muttered, checking his directive for errors. “They should be broken by the might of the Galactic Federation.”

But Earth thrived. Humans lived not in spite of their alien rulers, but because of them. And as Zorlax stood watching from his command ship, a young girl looked up and waved, her smile as bright as the stars from which he came, teaching him that perhaps, in the vast complexities of the universe, happiness was a far simpler matter than he had ever imagined.

The night skies never returned to their velvety black after the day we killed a God. Instead, they swirled with iridescent purples and haunting greens, a cosmic bruise spreading across the heavens. We, the accidental deicides, were left to reckon with our actions, with our newfound silence from the stars.

In a realm beyond our understanding, where time folds upon itself and space stretches like dough, the gods convened. Their forms were indescribable, shifting between dimensions and ideas, never settling on a shape comprehensible to the human mind. They communicated not in words but in ripples that altered reality, waves of thought that could birth galaxies or snuff them out.

"The Earthlings have ascended," one murmured, its voice a nebula unfolding.

"No," countered another, a flicker of dark matter, "they have merely shown the danger they pose."

"A God has fallen," a third intoned, its presence bending the light around it. "This is unprecedented."

In their midst, a void where the fallen had once been—an absence felt more acutely in the context of their immortality. The discourse was not about retribution, for what could they possibly do to a species that had slain a deity? It was about understanding, prevention, and perhaps, fear.

On Earth, news broadcasts played endlessly, looping footage of the cataclysmic battle, a clash that had shattered mountains and evaporated seas. Humanity had thrown everything at the cosmic horror that threatened to unravel their reality: nuclear arsenals, experimental weapons born of desperate science, prayers screamed into the void. And, miraculously, it had been enough.

In the small town of Eldridge, Anne-Marie, a retired schoolteacher, sat on her porch, looking up at the altered sky. She had lost her grandson in the fight, a bright-eyed physicist who had believed science would save them all. Now, she sifted through his letters, trying to find solace in his words, in his unwavering faith in humanity's potential.

"The other gods are watching us now," Anne-Marie read aloud to her old cat, Whiskers, who purred unperturbed at her side. Her grandson had written those words after the first sightings, when the world had laughed off the idea of ancient cosmic beings.

How different those words felt now.

The gods continued their silent council, each pondering the implications of Earth's defiance. Could they, should they intervene more directly, or was it time to cordon off this dangerous, unpredictable planet?

"Their potential is immense," the nebula-god finally conceded. "To harness such power—perhaps they are evolving beyond their cradle."

"But at what cost?" the dark matter flickered. "They wield the power of ruin."

The decision was made to watch, to wait. Earth would be quarantined, observed from afar, a case study in the cosmic ledger.

Back on her porch, Anne-Marie folded the letter, setting it beside her. The sky pulsed softly above, a reminder of their new reality. Humanity had killed a God, but at what cost? She gazed at the stars, her heart a blend of pride and sorrow, understanding at last the weight of their victory.

As the gods watched in silence, humanity embarked on its uncertain future, the heirs to a legacy of both greatness and terror. The night skies, bruised yet beautiful, watched right back.

Column 3: Instead of the Monkey’s Paw, you find the Clown’s Nose, which instead of granting your wish in the worst way possible will grant it in the funniest way.
Column 4:
In the quiet town of Pineridge, hidden behind curling ivy and whispered superstitions, there lay an eccentric little shop that sold oddities and artifacts, each with its own peculiar history. Among these curiosities was an item that had just arrived: a red, rubber clown’s nose nestled in an ancient, velvet-lined box. The shopkeeper, Mr. Tivoli, a man of considerable years and a mischievous twinkle in his eye, placed the box on the top shelf, behind a dusty sign that read “Clown’s Nose—Wish at Your Own Risk.”

Ellie, a young woman with a penchant for peculiar things, stumbled upon the shop on a rainy Thursday afternoon. Intrigued by the odd assortment of items, her eyes eventually rested on the red nose. Mr. Tivoli, noticing her interest, warned, “That’s no ordinary nose, my dear. It grants wishes, but in ways you might not expect. All in good humor, of course.”

With a mix of skepticism and curiosity, Ellie purchased the nose, ignoring the faint chuckles that seemed to echo from the walls as she left.

Back at home, Ellie examined the nose, its rubber surface smooth and oddly warm to the touch. Remembering Mr. Tivoli’s words, she thought of something harmless to wish for. “I wish my brother would lighten up a bit. He’s always so serious,” she mused aloud, giving the nose a tentative squeeze.

The next morning, Ellie’s brother, Michael, a stern accountant by profession, stepped into his office only to find every single document, spreadsheet, and even his digital files had been turned into elaborate coloring book pages. His colleagues, initially bewildered, soon found themselves laughing uncontrollably as Michael stood there, mouth agape, holding a financial report turned into a page featuring cartoonish dollar bills and piggy banks begging to be colored.

Word of the nose's powers spread, and soon Ellie’s friends came calling, each eager to make their own humorous wish. Sarah, who always lamented her lack of dance skills, wished to become a better dancer. At her next social outing, as she took to the dance floor, her movements mirrored the most exaggerated and comical dance steps from classic cartoons, earning roars of laughter and applause from the crowd.

Tom, who dreaded public speaking, wished to overcome his fear. At his next presentation, every time he felt nervous, his tie would automatically tighten, making his voice squeak in a high-pitched tone, turning his anxiety into a comedy act that had the whole room in stitches.

As for Ellie, the joy of seeing life infused with unexpected laughter was a gift unlike any other. Yet, she wondered about the limit of the nose's abilities. On a particularly quiet evening, she held the nose once more, a contemplative look in her eyes. “I wish to find someone who makes me laugh and loves me for who I am,” she whispered, not entirely sure what to expect.

The following day, while walking through the park, a playful dog bounded up to her, followed by its chuckling owner apologizing profusely. Between laughs and shared stories, something clicked. It wasn’t just the funny way they met, but the immediate warmth and understanding between them. The nose had worked its magic once more, bringing joy not just in the moment, but promising much more for the future.

Column 3: A centuries old vampire gets really into video games because playing a character who can walk around in the sun is the closest thing they have to experiencing the day again in centuries.
Column 4: Elias hadn’t touched daylight in 237 years. Not since the fever took his sister, and he’d stumbled into that crypt, half-delirious, bargaining with shadows. Now he lived in a studio above a Brooklyn bodega, the blinds sealed with duct tape. His skin smelled of old paper and the ozone crackle of CRT monitors.  The game was called Sunhaven Acres. A farming simulator. He’d bought it ironically, then become obsessed.  His avatar, Henry, wore overalls and a straw hat. Each morning, Henry stepped onto a pixelated porch, stretched, and yawned at a sunrise rendered in 8-bit gold. Elias would lean close, the monitor’s glow etching his gaunt face blue, and guide Henry through chores—tilling soil, milking cows, tossing feed to chickens that clucked in tinny MIDI. At noon, Henry napped under an oak tree while light dappled his overalls. Elias never skipped this part. He’d watch the screen until his eyes burned, imagining warmth on his neck.  “You’re always online,” messaged Marisol89, a fellow player. Her avatar wore a witch hat and sold enchanted turnips.  “Night owl,” Elias typed. His fingers hesitated. Night was too small a word.  The game’s nights were brief, just ten minutes of starry sky before dawn. Elias hated them. He’d send Henry to bed early, resetting the cycle. Once, Marisol89 asked why he never visited her night market. “Bad eyes,” he lied. “The dark strains them.”  When the shutdown notice came—Sunhaven Acres servers closing permanently June 1st—Elias drank three bags of O-negative and smashed his mug. Shards glittered like the chandeliers he’d known in Versailles. He logged on at 4:58 AM, one hour before server death.  Marisol89 was waiting by the virtual lake. “Last sunrise,” she said. Her avatar held a lantern.  Henry stood still as the horizon blushed. Elias’s hand hovered over the keyboard. Somewhere below, a garbage truck beeped. A drunk couple argued in Spanish. The city was waking up, and he would soon retreat to his coffin—a modified refrigerator lined with blackout curtains.  “Why the farming thing?” Marisol89 asked. “You never even grow crops.”  Elias made Henry kneel, a glitchy animation. The first sunbeam crested the hills. “Reminds me of my sister’s garden,” he typed. True, but incomplete. Clara had grown rosemary and lavender. She’d believed sunlight cured melancholy.  The server clock blinked 5:59. Elias leaned until his forehead touched the screen. The pixels blurred. For a moment, he could almost feel it—the way Clara used to grab his wrist, pulling him into meadows, her laugh bright and scolding. You’ll turn to stone, reading all day!  At 6:00 AM, the screen died. Error 404: Sunrise Not Found.  Downstairs, the bodega’s awning rattled up. Sunlight sliced the alley. Elias pressed a palm to the window’s edge, watching smoke curl from his seared skin. He’d done this every June 1st since 1983. A birthday ritual.  By dusk, the blisters would heal. He’d buy another game—Azure Skies, maybe, or Daybreak Chronicles. For now, he closed his eyes and let the pain ferment into memory. Clara’s garden. The way noon smelled when you weren’t afraid of it.  Somewhere, a child laughed. Elias bared his fangs at the empty room, tasting old blood and older longing. The monitor’s afterimage lingered behind his lids: a phantom sun, blue as a vein, fading.

Column 3: A psychic alien who feeds on dreams comes to Earth for the first time. Turns out humans are the only sentients in the galaxy that have nightmares.
Column 4: The first time it tastes a nightmare, the alien chokes.  It had expected pastel reveries, the sugary mists of Earth’s dreamscape. Instead, it gags on bile and smoke, on the coppery tang of phantom blood. Humans, it realizes, trembling behind the borrowed face of a gas station attendant, carry their hells inside them.  The alien’s species thrives on the soft hum of contentment—the dreams of a thousand placid civilizations, all pastel and predictable. But this... this is a symphony of teeth. A woman at Pump 3 clutches her coffee, her mind a battleground: her son’s crib empty again, his laughter curdling into sirens. The alien staggers, flooded by her grief. It’s alive. It’s alive in a way no dream has ever been.  By dawn, it’s addicted.  It finds her in the parking lot of a 24-hour diner. Marlene, 58, her hair still streaked with the burgundy of younger years. She dreams awake now—fingers drumming the steering wheel, eyes darting to rearview mirrors. The alien slips into the passenger seat, its form rippling like a mirage.  “Mind if I join?” it asks, though permission is irrelevant.  Marlene’s nightmare is a living thing: her brother’s Ford submerged in Lake Pontchartrain, his knuckles white on the wheel. She was twelve. She survived.  “You’re not real,” she mutters, knuckles matching her brother’s.  The alien feasts. Agony sears its throat, but beneath the rot, it finds something else—the frantic pulse of survival, the raw want to wake up. It’s grotesque. It’s exquisite.  Nights blur. The alien forgets to shed Marlene’s skin.  They drive. She talks in fragments: the way her brother’s voice cracks in her memory, the paramedic who called her “honey” as he wrapped her in foil. The alien’s hunger sharpens, but so does a nagging ache—a craving not for the nightmare, but for the woman who rebuilds herself inside it.  “Why stay?” it asks one night, the highway stretching endless.  Marlene grips the wheel. “Where else would I go?”  The alien hesitates. Reveals a sliver of truth: “My kind… we drift. We consume.”  “Yeah?” She laughs, brittle. “Welcome to the club.”  It happens in Oklahoma. Marlene dreams awake, the Ford’s headlights slicing through darkness. The alien reaches for the nightmare—and recoils.  It’s different.  The water isn’t freezing. The dashboard glows softly. Her brother turns, smiling. “You did good,” he says, though he never spoke again.  Marlene’s cheeks are wet. “Took me decades to let him say that.”  The alien trembles. This isn’t consumption; it’s communion.  When the craving returns, the alien hesitates. It could find fresher pain—a veteran’s flashback, a widow’s restless bed. But here, in this rusted Taurus, there’s a new flavor beneath the ash: not the absence of fear, but the choice to swallow it whole.  “Stay,” Marlene says, not looking over.  The alien peels off its borrowed faces. Lets her see the void beneath, the hunger etched into its core.  Marlene nods. “Yeah,” she whispers. “Me too.”  They drive east, the road humming beneath them. The alien learns to savor the aftertaste of nightmares—the stubborn, unyielding dawn that follows.

Column 3: Aliens take over the Earth. They then announce that they will be forcing the humans to work a ‘tyrannical’ 4 hours a day 4 days a week in exchange for basic rights like housing. Needless to say they are very confused when the humans celebrate their new alien overlords
Column 4:
The game was called Sunhaven Acres. A farming simulator. He’d bought it ironically, then become obsessed.The hologram flickered above Town Hall, casting an emerald sheen on faces upturned like sun-starved flowers. The Zyrathi’s voice buzzed through translation devices implanted in every throat: “Four solar cycles weekly. Four hours daily. Compliance ensures sustenance modules and domicile allocations.”

A beat of silence. Then, laughter rolled through the crowd—wet, jagged, disbelieving. Someone began clapping. Clara felt the sound in her molars, a childhood memory surfacing: her father’s calloused hands applauding her mother’s third consecutive night shift at the hospital.

“They think they’re punishing us,” whispered Mr. Park beside her. His fingernails still bore the grease stains of twelve-hour shifts at the shuttered auto plant.

On her first work assignment, Clara scrubbed biofilm from hexagonal towers while the Zyrathi supervisor, Gloam, hovered behind her. Her scrubber whirred against translucent walls, revealing dizzying views of the resurrected prairie below.

“Your pulse elevates,” Gloam intoned, eyestalks quivering. “Explain this physiological response to leisure intervals.”

Clara paused. The translation implant itched. “You’re giving us six hours back each day. Sir.”

“Correct. To demonstrate our dominance.”

She bit her lip, hiding a smile. The towers’ anti-microbial sheen felt nothing like the Dollar General’s sticky floors, where she’d once stocked shelves until 2 AM while Luna’s babysitter texted She’s asking when you’ll be real home.

That evening, Clara cooked actual garlic—a luxury when the Walmart closed—as Luna chattered about Gloam’s “playtime protocols” requiring guardians to spend 19:00-20:30 with offspring.

“Mrs. Nguyen says they’re brainwashing us,” Luna said, kneading cookie dough with hands already steadier than her mother’s.

Clara inhaled steam from boiling pasta, her skull throbbing with the phantom weight of a customer service headset. “Old Mrs. Nguyen worked 80 years without a pension. Let her call this brainwashing.”

Gloam intercepted Clara at the hydration station. “Your peer group exhibits counterintuitive dopamine spikes during mandatory community gardens.”

Clara sipped her rationed electrolyte fluid, now uncontaminated with microplastics. “You ever see someone try to grow tomatoes in a meth lab parking lot?”

The alien’s bioluminescent stripes pulsed orange—the manual said this signaled profound confusion. Clara pocketed an extra seed packet, still marveling at vegetables that didn’t glow.

At the solstice reconditioning ceremony, Gloam presented Clara with a “model worker” medal. The crowd whooped. Later, she found the alien studying security footage of humans dancing in the ration line.

“Your species,” Gloam rasped, “responds to benevolent authoritarianism with...”

“Relief,” Clara said softly. The medal chilled her palm. Somewhere beyond the towers, Luna was biking through pesticide-free meadows with other children who no longer hoarded Adderall to survive school.

The Zyrathi’s eyestalks drooped. Clara understood then—they’d expected resistance, not this terrible human talent for mistaking armistice for peace. She pocketed the medal, its alloy forged from melted-down credit card readers, and walked home through air that no longer tasted of burning.

Column 3: Humanity is visited by a cosmic horror the likes of which has only been seen in Lovecraftian horror. In desperation, Earth throws everything we have at it, and, miraculously, the human race has killed a God. Somewhere in a realm beyond our understanding, the other gods speak of the event.
Column 4:
They found Him in the garden where the oldest prayers wilted, His shadow still pooling like spilled ink beneath the fig trees. The others arrived one by one, their forms shimmering at the edges—a headache of light, a sigh of smoke.

“They gnawed through His spine with machines,” said He Who Parts the Veil, plucking a rotten pomegranate from a branch. His voice was the crackle of glaciers calving. “Primitive things. Cogs and sparks.”

She Who Holds the Vastness knelt, her fingertips brushing the god-corpses’s wrist. The flesh there had already petrified into a black, volcanic glass. “You’re certain it wasn’t… another of us?”

“They crowned it a war,” said the One Cloaked in Falling Teeth. His laughter was a swarm of locusts. “Humans. They name everything. Even their terrors.”

A wind stirred, carrying the stench of burnt ozone and something sweeter beneath—sweat, maybe, or adrenaline. The garden’s horizon flickered, its usual timeless twilight now threaded with a feverish, electric blue.

“They’ll expect retribution,” murmured She Who Holds the Vastness. Her many eyes reflected the corpse’s jagged angles. “We should flood their cities. Unmake their laws of physics.”

He Who Parts the Veil crushed the pomegranate. Seeds like teeth spilled. “And if they win again?”

Silence. The fig trees trembled, shedding centuries of unanswered prayers—cure her, bring him home, let me live, let me die.

The youngest of them materialized last, a thing of fraying starlight and static. It had no true name, only a sound like a radio dial spun too fast. “They mourned Him,” it buzzed. “After. They lit fires and sang.”

The others turned.

“I lingered,” it said. “In the ash. Their voices… they didn’t sound victorious. They sounded guilty. Like children who’d broken a beloved toy.”

“Guilt,” sneered the One Cloaked in Falling Teeth. “A parasite emotion. It changes nothing.”

“Doesn’t it?” The youngest’s light pulsed. “They wept because they’d won. Because they finally saw the wound they’d made in the dark.”

She Who Holds the Vastness stood, her silhouette warping into something jagged and avian. “You’re suggesting we let this stand? That we allow vermin to think they can—”

“They know,” interrupted the youngest. “That’s the trap. Now they’ll always wonder what else they can kill. What else is killable.”

Another silence. The corpse’s shadow had begun to crystallize, creeping across the garden floor in jagged lattices. Somewhere, a prayer from 312 A.D. dissolved into moths.

“We’ll quarantine them,” said He Who Parts the Veil finally. “Let their planet fester in isolation. No more visitations, no more revelations.”

“Too late,” murmured the youngest. “They’ll come looking now. They’ll invent new machines. New reasons.”

The garden dimmed. The fig trees, sensing discord, began to fold their leaves.

“Then what?” snapped the One Cloaked in Falling Teeth. “You want us to fear them?”

The youngest drifted toward the corpse, its light grazing the glassy flesh. “I want us to understand. They didn’t slay Him because they hated gods. They slew Him because they needed gods. Needed to prove they could exist without us.”

A tremor passed through the garden. The horizon’s electric blue deepened, bleeding into the black.

She Who Holds the Vastness tilted her head. “You sound almost… fond.”

The youngest dimmed. “I’ve been listening too long.”

They left the corpse there. Let it become a monument, or a mountain, or a myth. Let the garden grow around it, strangling and strange.

But later, when the others had dissolved back into their realms, the youngest returned. It hovered over the shadow, now a sprawling obsidian scar, and did something none of them had done in eons.

It whispered a prayer.

His avatar, Henry, wore overalls and a straw hat. Each morning, Henry stepped onto a pixelated porch, stretched, and yawned at a sunrise rendered in 8-bit gold. Elias would lean close, the monitor’s glow etching his gaunt face blue, and guide Henry through chores—tilling soil, milking cows, tossing feed to chickens that clucked in tinny MIDI. He’d watch the screen until his eyes burned, imagining warmth on his neck.Martin found the nose in the breast pocket of suit #4—charcoal wool, double-vented, still warm from the dryer. The deceased had been a circus clown. "Natural causes," the file said, though Martin noted the man’s smile lines had outlived his actual smile by decades. The nose was cherry-red, rubbery, faintly sticky. He pressed it to his own face on a whim.

Click.

A sound like a whoopee cushion deflating. Then silence.

That night, in the embalming room’s antiseptic hush, Martin muttered, "Wouldn’t mind some company." His voice startled him. Thirty-seven, divorced, speaking to clown paraphernalia. The fluorescent lights buzzed.

The next morning, a troupe of unicyclists circled the chapel parking lot.

"Birthday party for a Mr. Albert Gunderson?" their leader asked, rainbow suspenders straining.

"There’s been a—" Martin began, but a minivan disgorged eight children clutching Goodwill tutus. A terrier in a cone-collar herded them inside.

The viewing for Mrs. Eleanor Riggs became a hybrid affair. Mourners in black sniffled beside toddlers hyped on Sprite. A girl in dinosaur pajamas left Cheez-It offerings at the casket. The terrier peed on Martin’s Oxfords.

"Chaos," he hissed later, scrubbing the leather.

Chaos, his ex-wife used to say, is just order you’re not brave enough to dance with. She’d twirled through their apartment in mismatched socks, trailing cinnamon and Leonard Cohen lyrics. Martin had measured coffee grounds level to the teaspoon.

By Thursday, three more "parties" arrived. A Quinceañera. A D&D group. A man claiming to be an amateur tightrope walker ("I just need height, man"). Each time, Martin’s protestations dissolved when children’s laughter ricocheted off the marble angels, when the D&D teens shyly asked about his work, when the tightrope enthusiast wept over his dead cat.

The nose glowed in his desk drawer.

On Saturday, a woman with peacock hair brought a ukulele. "Funeral for my brother," she said, eyeing the clown nose now perched on Martin’s clipboard. "He loved pratfalls. Once mailed himself to Fiji as a bit."

Martin adjusted his tie. "We usually recommend—"

"Play something sad," she interrupted. "But make it swing."

He strummed. She tap-danced. The mourners—half strangers from prior parties—swayed. Someone spilled Merlot on the Persian rug. Someone else laughed, high and startled, and Martin felt something in his chest uncrimp.

Later, alone with the nose, he pressed it to his face.

Click.

Nothing changed.

He laughed anyway—raw, creaky, like a porch swing needing oil. The refrigerators hummed along.

In the morning, he placed the nose in suit #4’s pocket before sealing the casket. The clown’s makeup looked less waxy now, almost mischievous. Outside, a juggler practiced with lacquered skulls from the display shelf.

"Not a permanent addition," Martin warned, but he held the door open wider.

Chaos, he was learning, had its own liturgy. You didn’t control it; you let it slip its hand into yours, sweaty and trusting, and followed where it led.

Column 3: A centuries old vampire gets really into video games because playing a character who can walk around in the sun is the closest thing they have to experiencing the day again in centuries.
Column 4:
The first time Victor stepped into the sun in over three hundred years, he almost wept.

The game was nothing special—a sprawling, open-world RPG with a silent protagonist and the usual quests to save kingdoms, slay beasts, collect meaningless trinkets. The kind of thing humans consumed to feel momentarily significant. But Victor didn’t care about the quests. He wandered. He lingered on cobblestone paths, letting the pixelated sun drench his character’s shoulders. He stood in golden wheat fields as the wind—programmed in tight, mathematical loops—whispered through the stalks. He followed the rising light from dawn to dusk, moving through the world like a man relearning the shape of something long lost.

His hands, pale and long-fingered, rested lightly on the controller. The screen bathed his face in soft, flickering light, a mockery of warmth.

It was enough.

For a while, at least.

Victor had been turned in 1682, when the world smelled of damp earth and woodsmoke, when the sky still felt enormous, and stars were pinpricks of something divine. He remembered summer days spent barefoot, remembered how heat sank into his bones, made his skin fever-warm by evening. He had forgotten how it felt to sweat. To burn. To squint against the midday glare.

This game—this silly, human invention—offered a shadow of that feeling. And he clung to it.

He played at dusk, when hunger gnawed at the edges of his restraint. He fed quickly, cleanly, and returned before the night could stretch too long, before loneliness crept in like rot. He found a strange kind of companionship in the NPCs—shopkeepers with looping lines, blacksmiths hammering the same molten blade for eternity. They were unchanging, like him.

But it wasn’t real.

And that was the problem.

One evening, Victor found himself hesitating before pressing start. His fingers hovered over the controller. A thought had begun to fester, ugly and undeniable:

He was running out of things to do.

The world inside the screen had its limits. He had already traced every road, memorized every village. He had climbed to the highest peaks, waded through the deepest rivers. He had walked in sunlight so many times that the illusion had begun to thin.

He didn’t want a simulation anymore.

He wanted the real thing.

For the first time in centuries, the thought of stepping into the sun did not fill him with fear. It filled him with something closer to relief.

What would it feel like?

Would it be agony, or something gentler? Would he crumble into ash, or would his body take a moment to understand—just a breath, just a heartbeat—before it gave way?

He turned off the game. The screen went dark, swallowing the golden light, leaving him in the cold glow of his apartment. He sat still for a long time.

Then, just before dawn, Victor unlocked the door and stepped outside.

Column 3: Aliens take over the Earth. They then announce that they will be forcing the humans to work a ‘tyrannical’ 4 hours a day 4 days a week in exchange for basic rights like housing. Needless to say they are very confused when the humans celebrate their new alien overlords
Column 4:
The first week after the occupation, people cried in the streets. Some out of terror, some out of relief. When the broadcast came—translated in a voice that was neither male nor female, neither warm nor cold—most of us braced for demands, for war camps or mass executions. Instead, the message was clear:

"Your former rulers failed you. We will not. All humans must now work four hours a day, four days a week. In return, you will be housed, clothed, and fed. These are the terms of your servitude."

At first, there was silence. Then, from somewhere in the crowd, laughter. Disbelieving, half-hysterical. Then more laughter, until whole cities were vibrating with it. People in fast-food uniforms, people in suits, people who had been slumped in exhaustion only moments ago—clutching each other, wheezing. The aliens watched from their enormous ships, their faceless forms tilted in what might have been confusion.

“They think we are mocking them,” the voice continued. “This is not a negotiation. Work is mandatory.”

A man near me had tears in his eyes. “They think—” he gasped. “They think this is tyranny.”

It took time for the aliens to understand. We had worked sixteen-hour shifts for nothing. We had sat in cubicles until our backs bent wrong. We had gone to bed clutching our stomachs because rent had eaten our paychecks whole. They were waiting for the panic, for the rebellion, for the desperate pleas of a species forced into servitude. Instead, they got brunch reservations and spontaneous dance parties in the streets.

By the second week, something had shifted. The aliens—the Efficient, as they called themselves—began appearing more frequently, watching, studying. They asked the humans assigned to their “labor division” strange questions.

“Why do you not resist?”

“Are you hiding your suffering?”

“Why do you not attempt escape?”

One of them—sleek and towering, its voice like static over gravel—approached a former warehouse worker. She was sunbathing on the steps of her government-provided housing.

“You were given a task. Yet you are not performing it,” the alien said.

She didn’t even open her eyes. “I already worked my four hours today.”

The creature paused. “And what will you do now?”

She stretched luxuriously. “I don’t know. Maybe I’ll go for a walk. Maybe I’ll start painting again.”

“Again?”

“I used to, before. But I was too tired.”

A long silence. “And now?”

She opened her eyes then, staring at the creature through dark sunglasses. “Now I have time.”

For the first time, the aliens seemed… troubled. They had anticipated resistance. But they had not anticipated this. They had not anticipated how quickly humans, freed from their endless grinding, would begin to transform.

By the third week, humans were building things—not under orders, not under threat, but simply because they could. Music swelled in the streets. Parents spent time with their children. Strangers gathered in parks, speaking of ideas.

The Efficient watched it all unfold, their voices murmuring through their invisible channels. Their confusion was growing into something else—something closer to fear.

By the fourth week, they delivered a new broadcast.

"We were wrong."

There was silence in the streets.

"You are not what we expected. You are dangerous in a way we did not foresee. If you do not work endlessly, if you are given rest—then you begin to think. To create. To dream."

Their great ships began to hum, the light shifting as if preparing for departure.

"We have decided: You must govern yourselves once more. We are leaving."

A pause.

"We do not wish to see what you become."

And just like that, they were gone.

That night, people gathered in the streets. We stood beneath the alien sky, beneath a universe that had blinked first. And, for the first time in generations, we looked toward the future—not with dread, but with the quiet, dangerous thrill of possibility.

Column 3: Humanity is visited by a cosmic horror the likes of which has only been seen in Lovecraftian horror. In desperation, Earth throws everything we have at it, and, miraculously, the human race has killed a God. Somewhere in a realm beyond our understanding, the other gods speak of the event.
Column 4:
It is spoken of in the places where silence has weight.

Among the slumbering colossi, in the fathomless voids where time is neither forward nor back but a churning cycle of unfathomable motion, they whisper. Not in words, for words are too thin to hold the gravity of what has happened. They speak in gravity itself, in the slow rupture of unseen tides, in the distortions of space where horror once made its home.

One of them is gone.

A thing that was never meant to be slain, something vast and endless, folded in upon itself and undone. The void where it resided is now raw and exposed, a wound that reality has yet to scab over. Its absence is a wrongness that ripples through realms beyond counting.

The beings who remain—who have neither name nor number—observe in stillness. They are patient, but patience does not mean indifference. For eons unmeasured, they have watched the little things that scuttle and breed and burn on that speck of spinning dirt. They have found them amusing in their agony, inventive in their despair. They have watched them war upon each other, clawing and raving with bloodied hands, desperate to define themselves against a universe that does not care.

But now—now these things have killed one of their own.

Not merely driven it back, not merely cowered and prayed in futility. No. They fought, and they won. They obliterated that which is beyond obliteration. They broke the spine of something that had never before known the threat of harm.

A quiet shifts between them. A gravity unmoors. Possibility—a concept they had never before needed to consider—presses against the edges of their endlessness.

“Accident,” one suggests, not in words, but in the collapsing of distant stars. A death-rattle of burning light.

“Instinct,” another counters, with the slowing decay of a black hole’s hunger.

“Will,” a third hums, and the fabric of things recoils.

That is what disturbs them most. Will is the domain of greater things. The crawling things were never meant to possess it beyond the flickering of their tiny, transient wars. Their rage was always meant to be impotent, their terror their defining trait. And yet, in that final moment—when the last shrieking call of their fallen kin had rung through the void—there had been something else. Not terror. Not desperation. But intent.

What does it mean when prey learns to devour? When the hunted sharpen their teeth? When creatures made for extinction decide, instead, to endure?

Another speaks—something slow, deep, a shift of pressure felt rather than heard.

“They will come for more.”

The thought is absurd. Laughable, if laughter were something such things could produce. The speck-bound creatures could not reach here. Could not grasp the true shape of what lay beyond their mortal sky. Could not even conceive of what they had done, not fully.

And yet.

There is a silence between them, vast and contemplative.

The wound remains open. The absence festers.

Somewhere, in the dark and unknowable places, a great and terrible thing considers, for the first time, the possibility of fear.

Elliot found it in a box of old costumes at the back of the thrift store, buried under moth-eaten capes and a plastic Viking helmet. A bright red clown nose, slightly worn but still elastic. When he picked it up, the cashier—a wiry woman with a face like a walnut—perked up.

“Oh,” she said, peering at him over her bifocals. “That’s a special one.”

“Special how?”

She pressed her lips together, as if deciding whether he deserved to know. Then she leaned in and whispered, “It grants wishes.”

Elliot snorted. “Like a genie?”

“Sort of,” she said, bagging it carefully, like it was something delicate, breakable. “But it has a sense of humor.”

It was two dollars. He bought it for the same reason anyone buys something dumb and cheap—for the possibility, however slim, of an interesting night.

Back at his apartment, Elliot sat at his kitchen table, twirling the nose between his fingers. He had nothing to lose. His ex-girlfriend was dating a guy who brewed his own kombucha, his job at the copy shop made him fantasize about office fires, and his landlord had just announced a rent hike.

He cleared his throat. “I wish for a million dollars.”

Nothing happened.

Then, from the hallway, he heard a strange rustling. He stood and opened the door. A single one-dollar bill lay at his feet. As he bent to pick it up, another floated down from the ceiling. Then another. And another.

He craned his neck. Wedged into the ceiling vent was a wriggling, full-sized man in a green leotard, stuffing money through the slats like a reverse ATM.

“HEY!” Elliot yelled.

The man turned, grinned, and gave him a thumbs-up. “Don’t worry, buddy! Only 999,997 to go!”

Elliot slammed the door.

The next night, he tried again.

“I wish my boss would quit.”

The following morning, he arrived at work to find a single, perfectly folded note taped to the register. It read:

Dear esteemed associates,
It is with a heavy heart that I must resign, effective immediately.
I have been called to a higher purpose.

There was no signature.

Elliot turned. “Where’s Greg?”

Jenna, the assistant manager, scrolled her phone with a dazed look. “Uh,” she said. “He’s currently in rural Nepal, training to be a yak whisperer.”

A quick Google search confirmed it: a shaky YouTube livestream showed Greg—former micromanaging tyrant, dedicated spreadsheet enthusiast—sitting cross-legged beside an enormous yak, speaking in low, reverent tones.

Elliot stared at the screen. “That… counts, I guess.”

By the end of the week, he was reckless.

“I wish to be irresistible to women.”

The next morning, he woke up and stretched—only to find his left hand gripping a perfect, glistening rotisserie chicken.

“What the—”

His right hand held another.

His entire bed was full of them.

At the bus stop, a woman sniffed the air and turned to him, eyes dark with hunger. “Oh my god,” she whispered.

Elliot ran.

Eventually, he accepted the rules. The nose granted wishes, but with the same logic as a dream: absurd, hilarious, technically correct. It was never cruel, but it was never quite what he expected.

He kept it in a drawer, next to his old apartment keys and a half-used book of stamps. Some nights, when he was feeling particularly stupid, he would take it out, press it to his face, and whisper something ridiculous just to see what happened next.

Column 4: The game’s nights were brief, just ten minutes of starry sky before dawn. Elias hated them. He’d send Henry to bed early, resetting the cycle. Once, Marisol89 asked why he never visited her night market. “Bad eyes,” he lied. “The dark strains them.”

When the shutdown notice came—Sunhaven Acres servers closing permanently June 1st—Elias drank three bags of O-negative and smashed his mug. Shards glittered like the chandeliers he’d known in Versailles. He logged on at 4:58 AM, one hour before server death.
Marisol89 was waiting by the virtual lake. “Last sunrise,” she said. Her avatar held a lantern.

Henry stood still as the horizon blushed. Elias’s hand hovered over the keyboard. Somewhere below, a garbage truck beeped. A drunk couple argued in Spanish. The city was waking up, and he would soon retreat to his coffin—a modified refrigerator lined with blackout curtains.
“Why the farming thing?” Marisol89 asked. “You never even grow crops.”

Elias made Henry kneel, a glitchy animation. The first sunbeam crested the hills. “Reminds me of my sister’s garden,” he typed. True, but incomplete. Clara had grown rosemary and lavender. She’d believed sunlight cured melancholy.

The server clock blinked 5:59. Elias leaned until his forehead touched the screen. The pixels blurred. For a moment, he could almost feel it—the way Clara used to grab his wrist, pulling him into meadows, her laugh bright and scolding. You’ll turn to stone, reading all day!
At 6:00 AM, the screen died. Error 404: Sunrise Not Found.

Downstairs, the bodega’s awning rattled up. Sunlight sliced the alley. Elias pressed a palm to the window’s edge, watching smoke curl from his seared skin. He’d done this every June 1st since 1983. A birthday ritual.

By dusk, the blisters would heal. He’d buy another game—Azure Skies, maybe, or Daybreak Chronicles. For now, he closed his eyes and let the pain ferment into memory. Clara’s garden. The way noon smelled when you weren’t afraid of it.
Somewhere, a child laughed. Elias bared his fangs at the empty room, tasting old blood and older longing. The monitor’s afterimage lingered behind his lids: a phantom sun, blue as a vein, fading.
